stops.name: Cairo, born to the house of al-Adil
stops.campa: Muhammad is born in Cairo, eldest son of al-Adil Sayf al-Din, brother of the great Salah al-Din. The uncle's name fills the house before the boy can walk: the retaker of Jerusalem, the breaker of the Franks at Hattin. Al-Adil governs for his brother, and the child is raised inside statecraft the way other boys are raised inside a trade, watching petitions read, watching armies mustered. He is given the throne-name al-Malik al-Kamil, the Perfect King, before he has done anything to earn it — a title the years will spend testing.

stops.name: Acre, knighted by King Richard
stops.campa: Through the long truce-talks of the crusade's last year, Richard Coeur-de-Lion treats with al-Adil over a marriage that might join Latin Jerusalem to Ayyubid Egypt: the English king's own sister Joan to be given to al-Adil, the kingdom shared between them under one crown. The match fails, but at Easter, back in Acre, Richard performs the one gesture that outlasts it: he girds the eleven-year-old son of al-Adil with the belt of knighthood, Frankish sword on a Muslim prince's shoulder, a courtesy between men who esteem each other's line before they esteem each other's faith.

stops.name: Harran, the young commander's first campaign
stops.campa: Sent east into the Jazira on his father's business, al-Kamil commands the siege of Mardin and is thrown back by the combined lords of Mosul, Sinjar and Jazirat ibn Umar. It is not the victory the family wants of Saladin's line, but he steadies the reverse: Harran is secured, the eastern march of the Ayyubid house held together while older men bicker over the succession left unsettled since Salah al-Din's death. The lesson he takes from this first field is the one that will define his sultanate — that consolidation outlasts conquest.

stops.name: Cairo, appointed viceroy of Egypt
stops.campa: Al-Adil, now sultan in his own right after the family's wars of succession, calls his eldest son back from the eastern marches and sets him as na'ib, viceroy, over Egypt — the richest province of the house and the one nearest the sea the Franks command. Al-Kamil is twenty. For eighteen years he will govern Cairo in his father's name: judging disputes, keeping the granaries, watching the coast where every generation a new fleet of crusaders lands. It is the longest apprenticeship any Ayyubid prince has served, and it makes him, before he is ever sultan, the most practiced ruler of his line.

stops.name: Cairo, the citadel raised over the city
stops.campa: As viceroy al-Kamil oversees the great work his uncle Salah al-Din began and his father continues: the Citadel of the Mountain rising over Cairo, its Ayyubid walls enclosing a seat of government meant to outlast any single sultan. He issues decrees in his own name from within it, dismisses and appoints ministers — the fall of the powerful vizier Ibn Shukr is laid at his door — and learns to rule not as a soldier holding a camp but as a prince holding a capital. The citadel will stand through every dynasty that follows the Ayyubids; it is the one monument of this reign that needs no treaty to survive.

stops.name: Cairo, the Kamiliyya founded for the traditionists
stops.campa: Amid the wars this sultan founds, in the Jamaliyya quarter of Cairo, the Madrasa al-Kamiliyya: a house given wholly to the study of the hadith, the sayings of the Prophet, the discipline the learned call dar al-hadith. It becomes within a generation the most respected school of traditionists in Egypt. He is a man, his own chroniclers say, who loves the company of scholars more than the company of flatterers, who would rather argue a fine point of law or astronomy over a meal than be praised for victories he counts, in his own reckoning, as burdens rather than glories.

stops.name: Damietta camp, the crown falls to him mid-siege
stops.campa: The Fifth Crusade's fleet has been anchored off Damietta since May, and in late August the crusaders storm the chain tower that bars the Nile, opening the river to their ships. Days later, in the field before the threatened city, word comes that al-Adil has died in Syria. Al-Kamil, already commanding Egypt's defense as viceroy, is now sultan in fact as well as name, inheriting a father's throne and a father's unfinished war in the same week, the crown descending on him between one assault and the next with no time allowed to mourn it.

stops.name: Damietta camp, the conspiracy of Ibn al-Mashtub
stops.campa: In the depth of the siege, with the army's confidence shaken, the amir Imad al-Din ibn al-Mashtub, commander of the Kurdish Hakkari regiment, conspires to unseat al-Kamil for his younger, more biddable brother al-Faiz. Warned in time, the sultan flees his own camp by night rather than face the plotters, and in the chaos the crusaders press their advantage and tighten their grip on Damietta. He considers, for a dark hour, sailing on to Yemen where his son already rules, and leaving Egypt to whoever can hold it — the nearest this reign comes to simply walking away from the throne.

stops.name: Damietta camp, al-Mu'azzam's ride, the conspiracy broken
stops.campa: His brother al-Mu'azzam Isa, lord of Damascus, rides down from Syria with reinforcements the moment word of the plot reaches him, and the conspiracy collapses as quickly as it rose: Ibn al-Mashtub is arrested and exiled, al-Faiz sent quietly home, the army made whole again around its rightful sultan. Al-Kamil returns to the siege lines a man twice tested in his first winter as ruler — once by the Franks outside the camp, once by his own captains within it — and twice, by his brother's loyalty, delivered.

stops.name: Fariskur, the first offer of Jerusalem
stops.campa: After a costly action near Fariskur, al-Kamil sends across the lines a proposal the crusader camp has not dared hope for: he will restore Jerusalem itself, rebuild what has been thrown down, return relics of the True Cross taken since Hattin, and grant a long truce, if only the army will leave Egypt in peace. His own captains think him mad to give away Salah al-Din's great prize so cheaply; he thinks the exchange plain arithmetic — a half-ruined city bought back against the granary of his kingdom. The legate Pelagius, certain of total victory, refuses to hear it.

stops.name: Fariskur, the friar from Assisi
stops.campa: Two unarmed men are dragged into his tent crying Soldan, beaten and chained by soldiers who take them for spies: a small friar in a patched habit, Francesco of Assisi, and his companion Illuminato. Al-Kamil, expecting envoys or renegades, finds instead a man offering to walk into fire beside his own imams to prove which faith God favors. He will not light the fire, but he will not let the little man be harmed either. For days he keeps him near, listens to him preach without anger, offers gifts he refuses, and sends him back under armed escort, unconverted and unharmed, asking only a prayer in return.
stops.quote: Pray for me, that God may deign to reveal to me the law and the faith which is more pleasing to Him.
stops.quote_source: Jacques de Vitry, Historia occidentalis (the sultan's parting words to Francis, the earliest witness; retold in Bonaventure, Legenda Maior IX)

stops.name: Damietta, the city falls, the dead in the streets
stops.campa: Damietta falls not to storm but to starvation: plague and famine have already emptied the city of half its people, and when the crusaders finally climb the undefended walls in the night they find streets carpeted with the dead, too weak even to be buried by the living who remain. Al-Kamil withdraws his broken army south to al-Mansurah rather than lose it entirely defending a corpse of a city. He has lost the greatest port of Egypt to a siege sixteen months long, and the offer of Jerusalem he made before its fall he does not withdraw — he repeats it, again and again, through the crusader winter to come.
